name: Transferring knowledge across contexts
gist: Understanding when knowledge learned in one setting can help in a different setting, and the conditions under which transfer learning succeeds or fails.
explain: A model trained to recognize dogs in photographs can often recognize dogs in paintings, sketches, or even cartoons, even though it was never trained on these styles, which suggests that the model learned something general about dog-ness rather than specific pixel patterns. A language model trained on English text can often answer questions about historical events it was not explicitly trained to answer because it learned underlying reasoning patterns. A robot trained to grasp cylinders can often grasp boxes, even though it was trained with different objects. Transfer learning — using knowledge learned in one context to improve learning in another context — is one of the most useful and common techniques in machine learning, meaning many practitioners rely on it to reduce training time and data requirements. Yet when does transfer help and when does it hurt, since sometimes knowledge from the old task misleads rather than guides, wasting the learner's time on false patterns? This subtheme investigates: what conditions allow knowledge to transfer safely so you can rely on it, and how do you measure whether transfer is actually occurring rather than just coincidental similarity by comparing to a baseline, which determines whether an experiment actually validates the technique?

The difficulty is determining what transfers and what does not. Low-level features like edges and textures in images transfer well across visual domains, but high-level concepts may not (a model trained to recognize dogs may struggle with cats if it learned dog-specific features). Transfer can also fail silently: a model may perform well on the new task not because of genuine transfer but because both tasks are easy. Negative transfer occurs when knowledge from the source task interferes with learning the target task — the model must unlearn incorrect assumptions. Additionally, you must quantify how different two tasks are; two tasks that seem similar might require different models, while two tasks that seem different might share deep structure.

Researchers analyze source and target domains, measuring their similarity through theoretical and empirical metrics to quantify how close they are. They study domain adaptation techniques that adjust a model trained on one domain to work on a different domain with limited retraining. They investigate feature reuse — what parts of a model (layers, connection-weight patterns or decision nodes, individual neurons) encode transferable knowledge and which parts are task-specific — so they know what can move and what must stay fixed. They analyze when transfer helps by comparing transfer learning to training from scratch, isolating the benefit of the source task. They also study negative transfer, identifying which source tasks hurt which target tasks and how to select source tasks wisely, to avoid picking knowledge that misleads. The work includes investigating task relationships and hierarchies, asking whether learning on many related tasks jointly (multitask learning) improves performance compared to learning each task independently, since tasks may help or hinder each other in unexpected ways.

papers.title: On the Bayes Inconsistency of Disagreement Discrepancy Surrogates
papers.contribution: Provides more accurate and robust estimates of disagreement discrepancy than existing approaches, particularly under adversarial conditions.

papers.title: Quantifying Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation in the Presence of Domain Shift
papers.contribution: The analysis shows that even with substantial domain differences there exists a regime where the student achieves superior generalization and identifies a crossed double descent phenomenon.

papers.title: Temporal Generalization: A Reality Check
papers.contribution: Empirically demonstrates that none of the evaluated methods consistently outperforms the simple baseline of using the latest model parameters across scenarios, cautioning against temporal generalization claims.

papers.title: The Generalization Spectrum: A Chromatographic Approach to Evaluating Learning Algorithms
papers.contribution: Reveals that RL converts memorization to near-transfer more efficiently than SFT, ICL exhibits strong correspondence-dependent transfer, and local improvements don't expand generalization radius.

papers.title: Understanding Transfer Learning of RNA Foundation Models on Downstream Tasks
papers.contribution: Demonstrates frozen representations are not universally transferable; pretraining benefits via optimization initialization when objectives align, accelerating convergence to flatter minima.

papers.title: Beyond Spectra: Eigenvector Overlaps in Loss Geometry
papers.contribution: Reveals eigenspace alignment as controlling multiple descent peaks rather than Hessian ill-conditioning; develops algorithms estimating overlap functionals validated on ResNet-20 and CIFAR10.

papers.title: Coupled Training with Privileged Information and Unlabeled Data
papers.contribution: Avoids failures and consistently outperforms two-step baselines on synthetic and medical prediction tasks with theoretical guarantees.

papers.title: Covariate-Guided Clusterwise Linear Regression for Generalization to Unseen Data
papers.contribution: Method spans spectrum from global to instance-wise fits with convergence guarantees and PAC-style excess-risk bounds.

papers.title: Geometric Rate–Distortion Invariance for Domain Generalization
papers.contribution: RDI provides finite-sample stability guarantees under bounded shifts and is competitive with strong baselines on DomainBed with ablations confirming both alignment and complexity control are necessary.

papers.title: Hedging on the Frontier: Learning New Tasks with Few Samples
papers.contribution: Can prune model class based on monotonicity and hedge on frontier geometry of available trade-offs for improved few-shot learning.

papers.title: Identifying Partially Observed Causal Models from Heterogeneous/Nonstationary Data
papers.contribution: Proves distributional constraints in heterogeneous/nonstationary cases are equivalent to homogeneous cases and provides methods to identify causal structure and variables with distribution shifts.

papers.title: Neyman-Pearson Classification under Both Null and Alternative Distributions Shift
papers.contribution: Provides statistical and computational guarantees for improved Type-I and Type-II errors under simultaneous distribution shifts in both distributions.

papers.title: On the Computational Complexity of Performative Prediction
papers.contribution: A sharp phase transition reveals PPAD-hardness for performative prediction, equivalent to Nash equilibria in general-sum games, and strategic classification local optima are PLS-hard.

papers.title: Particle Flow for Learning from Label Proportions
papers.contribution: Demonstrates effectiveness on tabular and image datasets while providing theoretical convergence guarantees and identifying label proportion gap and diversity as critical factors.

papers.title: Positive Distribution Shift as a Framework for Understanding Tractable Learning
papers.contribution: Shows certain hard function classes become learnable under PDS using standard gradient-based training; computational benefits often outweigh statistical ones.

papers.title: Regularized Discriminative Alignment for Deep Representations under Label Shift
papers.contribution: Significantly outperforms baselines in both data-scarce and extreme-shift regimes with superior robustness and accuracy.

papers.title: Residual Feature Integration is Sufficient to Prevent Negative Transfer
papers.contribution: Proves convergence rate no worse than training from scratch under informative distributions up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Testing For Distribution Shifts with Conditional Conformal Test Martingales
papers.contribution: Anytime-valid type-I error control, asymptotic power one, bounded expected detection delay, and faster shift detection than standard CTMs.

papers.title: Transfer Learning in Nonparametric Regression with Deep ReLU Networks
papers.contribution: Establishes upper bounds on L2 error and derives explicit convergence rates for deep ReLU networks under hierarchical composition models, demonstrating ability to overcome curse of dimensionality.

papers.title: When More Data Doesn't Help: Limits of Adaptation in Multitask Learning
papers.contribution: Proves an impossibility result demonstrating that the hardness of multitask learning cannot be overcome by having abundant data per task alone.
